posts.quote: THE FIRST HARD FROST MEANT DAD SHUT OFF THE OUTSIDE FAUCET, AND THAT WAS HOW WE KNEW WINTER HAD OFFICIALLY ARRIVED.
posts.caption: There was a morning every November when Dad walked outside before breakfast, looked at the white grass, and said nothing at all. Then he went down to the basement with a wrench and turned the shutoff valve under the stairs. He opened the faucet on the side of the house to let the last of the water run out, and he left it open all winter so the pipe could not split. The hose got coiled up and hung on its nail in the garage, and that was the end of washing the car. We never needed a calendar to tell us the season had changed. We just watched which tool Dad carried out of the house.
posts.first: Dad kept a little tag tied to that valve that said OFF in his blocky capital letters, and he retied it every fall. When I bought my own house years later I found myself doing the same thing without being told. Some habits come with the toolbox.

posts.quote: THE MANTEL CLOCK WAS WOUND EVERY SUNDAY NIGHT, AND ONLY ONE PERSON IN THE HOUSE HAD THE KEY.
posts.caption: It sat in the exact middle of the mantel, between a framed wedding photograph and a glass candy dish nobody ever emptied. The key lived in the drawer of the little table beside Grandpa's chair, and Sunday night after supper he opened the glass door and gave it his slow, careful turns. Everyone else in the house was allowed to look at the clock and tell the time. Nobody was allowed to touch the hands, and nobody had to be told twice. It struck the hour a few seconds late for forty years, and we set our watches by it anyway.
posts.first: Our clock chimed a half note flat on the quarter hour, and I could pick out that sound from another room with my eyes closed. After Grandpa passed, my father wound it every Sunday without saying why. It still runs in his front room.

posts.quote: THE CAFETERIA LADY / A HAIRNET, A LADLE, AND A SECOND ROLL FOR THE KID WHO NEEDED IT
posts.caption: She stood behind the steam table in a white apron and a hairnet, and she had a ladle in her hand like a judge holding a gavel. She did not say much, but she looked at every kid who came through the line, and she remembered who was growing too fast and who had skipped breakfast. A second roll would slide onto a few trays without a word, and the kid it was meant for always knew. She wrote nothing down and asked for nothing back. Years later it is the roll I remember better than any lesson in that building.
posts.first: The lady in our school was Mrs. Pruitt, and she called every boy sweetheart, even the ones who needed a haircut. I carried my tray to the same table every day and she never once got the milk wrong. She retired the year I left for high school, and it felt like the building should have said something.

posts.quote: Grandpa folded the newspaper into quarters so he could read it one-handed at the breakfast table.
posts.first: He held his coffee in the other hand and never spilled a drop. The paper came out of its folds with a sound I can still hear, a quick snap and then silence. My grandmother said it was the only time he sat still all day.

posts.quote: WE SLEPT ON THE SCREENED PORCH IN JULY, AND THE CRICKETS NEVER ONCE TOOK A NIGHT OFF.
posts.caption: On the hottest nights of July, Mom dragged the cots out to the screened porch and the whole house moved outside. The mattresses smelled like cedar and old canvas, and the sheets were damp from the heat before you even lay down. Moths ticked against the screen and a box fan turned slowly in the corner. Somewhere out in the yard the crickets started up and did not stop until the sun was almost in your face. You were told to go to sleep, but nobody really slept until the air turned cool just before morning.
posts.first: My brother and I kept a flashlight under the pillow and read comics until the batteries went yellow. The screen door had a spring that sang when it opened, and Mom could tell from the sound exactly who was sneaking in for a glass of water. Those nights are still the longest summer I own.

posts.quote: THE HOOP OVER THE GARAGE HAD NO NET, AND EVERY KID ON THE BLOCK KNEW EXACTLY HOW THE BALL BOUNCED OFF THAT RIM.
posts.caption: Dad bolted a plywood backboard over the garage door one Saturday and painted a white square on it with leftover house paint. The rim was bent a little on the left side from a ladder that slipped, and nobody ever fixed it. By August every kid on the block understood its moods better than their own homework. A shot that hit the left side kicked sideways into the hydrangea, and a shot that hit the back came straight down like it had been called home. You could tell a stranger on our driveway by the way he missed.
posts.first: The net lasted about a week the summer Dad put it up, and then the rim looked the way it was always going to look. I knew that bounce so well I could have made a free throw blindfolded. The paint is still faintly visible on that board.

posts.quote: THE CLARINET CAME HOME IN A CASE THAT SMELLED LIKE OLD VELVET, AND THE PRACTICING WAS A WHOLE FAMILY'S PROBLEM.
posts.caption: The case had a latch that snapped like a mousetrap, and inside the velvet lining was the color of a wine stain. For a month it was one note, then two, then something close to a scale on a good day. Mom kept the radio on in the kitchen louder than usual and Dad suddenly remembered the garage needed sweeping. The dog went under the bed and stayed there until supper. Nobody said a word against it, because everybody had agreed without speaking that this was how a musician got made.
posts.first: I played third chair in the school band for exactly two years and never got any better than adequate. My father still says the best thing I ever played was the last note of the spring concert, because that meant it was over. He kept the program in his wallet anyway.

posts.quote: The spare key lived under the flowerpot, and the whole neighborhood pretended not to know.
posts.first: Ours was a chipped clay pot with a geranium that never quite died. I locked myself out twice and the key was always right where it should be. I never saw anyone tell the mailman, but I think he knew too.

posts.quote: THE TELEGRAM / A YELLOW ENVELOPE, A KNOCK AT THE DOOR, AND NEWS THAT COULDN'T WAIT
posts.caption: Most of the time a knock at the door meant a neighbor or the paperboy collecting. But when a boy on a bicycle stood on the step holding a thin yellow envelope, the whole house went quiet. Mom wiped her hands on her apron before she took it, and she read it standing right there in the doorway. Sometimes it was good news and the kitchen filled with noise. Sometimes it was not, and she folded it very carefully and put it in her pocket. Either way, you remembered the color of that paper for the rest of your life.
posts.first: My grandmother kept one telegram in her Bible for fifty years, a short one announcing my uncle's safe arrival somewhere overseas. The paper had gone soft as cloth at the folds. She said it was the shortest letter she ever loved.

posts.quote: THE YARDSTICK FROM THE FEED STORE WAS THE ONLY RULER IN THE HOUSE, AND IT MEASURED EVERYTHING FROM CURTAINS TO CAKE PANS TO PLANTING ROWS.
posts.caption: It was free with a purchase, and it had the name of the feed store stamped along one edge in red letters. It hung from a nail in the pantry, between the dish towels and the flyswatter. Mom used it to hem curtains, Dad used it to lay out the tomato rows, and I used it on one memorable occasion as a sword. The inches were worn so smooth at the middle that you had to tilt it toward the window to read them. Nothing in that house was ever measured with anything else.
posts.first: The feed store's name is almost gone from ours now, but I can still make out the first two letters. It measured my height every birthday until the pencil marks climbed past it. I keep it in my own pantry on a nail.
